appraisal_events.evidence: « Robert a jeté cela sans reprendre haleine, on pouvait à peine distinguer qu'il y avait du latin là dedans, il avait l'air d'un personnage du Malade imaginaire ! »
appraisal_events.explanation: Prompted by the duc's challenge (« que Madame demande à Oriane si j'exagère »), the duchesse entertains the princesse de Parme by turning Saint-Loup's Latin epigram into a joke: it took twenty questions and linguists to reconstitute what he gabbled, and he sounded like a Molière quack. The absent Saint-Loup is made comically ridiculous while the duchesse scores as the table's wit.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Cette Rachel m'a parlé de vous, elle m'a dit que le petit Saint-Loup vous adorait, vous préférait même à elle », me dit le prince Von
appraisal_events.explanation: The prince Von relays to the narrator Rachel's report that Saint-Loup adores him and prefers him even to his own mistress, an explicitly comparative preference that raises the narrator over Rachel in Saint-Loup's affections. The narrator reports the compliment without endorsing it.

status_effects.explanation: His learned Latin is recounted as unintelligible gabble, so his standing as a speaker is locally deflated before the assembled guests.
She holds the table and the Highness's attention, supplying the reconstructed phrase and the Molière comparison that make the anecdote land.
He is reported as adored by Saint-Loup and preferred to Saint-Loup's mistress, which locally puts him ahead in that attachment.
By her own reported words she is ranked below the narrator in Saint-Loup's preference.

ambiguities: The speaker of the Latin anecdote is not tagged: the duc has just said « Il parle latin » and invites « que Madame demande à Oriane si j'exagère », so the following « Mais comment, madame… » is read here as Oriane confirming him; if it is instead the duc continuing, the source of E1 shifts to him and the duchesse's rhetorical gain disappears.

The mockery of Saint-Loup is affectionate salon banter and does credit him with an actual Latin epigram, so it could be read as backhanded admiration rather than diminishment; the emphasis on unintelligibility and the Malade imaginaire comparison makes diminishment the stronger reading.
